items.title: Morning Digest: All departing U.S. flights grounded due to communication outage; Microsoft outage hits businesses worldwide, India feels impact, and more - The Hindu
items.excerpt: Published - November ... #### All departing U.S. flights grounded due to communication outage All flights in the U.S. were grounded on Friday (November 13, 2026), sparking travel chaos across the vast country, after what government officials said was a major communications outage, insisting it was not the result of any “nefarious attack.” The nationwide stop left tens of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before departure by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events. The incident marked only the second time such an alert was given in U.S. airspace since the 9/11 attacks. #### Microsoft outage hits businesses worldwide; India feels impact The global disruption of multiple Microsoft services, which began on Thursday (November 12, 2026) and continued late into Friday (November 13, 2026), affected several Indian businesses’ internal communications and customer-facing operations. In its latest update on Friday (November 13, 2026), the company said it was making progress in fixing the outage, which has affected email access and workplace applications in businesses, public services, and other organisations across the globe. In India, the disruptions affected businesses from startups to multinational corporations. Follow LIVE updates here. #### Tanker hits a river cruise boat on Mississippi River in New Orleans; rescue operations under way A tanker in New Orleans that apparently lost its steering slammed into a docked river cruise boat with 180 people aboard on Friday (November 13, 2026), the Mayor said. All aboard survived after the crash prompted a massive rescue operation for passengers and crew who plunged into the Mississippi River as the ship took on water and began to topple over. Video from the scene showed the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker hit the cruise boat while it was docked as metal and glass crashed and crunched. #### In major breakthrough, U.S. assures India of comparative tariff advantage over its competitors In a significant breakthrough towards the conclusion of the India-U.S. interim deal on trade, the U.S. has assured India of a comparative advantage over its competitors once it finalises its tariff structure, a senior official in the Ministry of Commerce and Industry said, adding that both sides are working to complete the deal by the end of the current financial year. Indian officials have repeatedly been saying that India would move ahead with a deal only if the U.S. assured it of a comparative advantage, as was agreed to in the February 2026 joint statement between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and U.S. President Donald Trump. ... #### Students among 24 dead in bus-truck collision in Assam’s Kaziranga College students were among 24 people killed when a minibus collided head-on with a container truck at Rangajan near Kaziranga National Park in eastern Assam’s Golaghat district on Friday (November 13, 2026). Officials said 39 people, including the driver, were on board when the accident occurred at around 1 p.m. on National Highway-715. The spot is about 230 km east of Guwahati. #### Delhi overtakes Lahore as world’s most polluted city as air quality drops Delhi overtook Lahore to become the world’s ‌most polluted city on Friday (November 13, 2026), with ​air quality reaching hazardous ⁠levels and visibility dropping as smog blanketed the city of 20 million people. Air quality index (AQI) in Delhi was “hazardous” at 334, making ‌it the most polluted ‌major city, according to Swiss ⁠group IQAir, which measures air quality levels based on the concentration of toxins ... #### Turkiye, Qatar sign mutual defence agreement, Turkish presidency says Turkiye and ​Qatar signed a mutual defence agreement on Friday (November 13, 2026), ‌the office of President Tayyip Erdogan said, ​as the Turkish leader ⁠met the Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani in Istanbul. “President Erdogan stated that we ‌would continue working together to prevent the resurgence of war in ‌the Gulf region and establish a ‌basis ⁠for dialogue and achieve peace,” ⁠the presidency said in a statement on X, which did not provide details on the defence accord.

items.title: World News Live Updates: Delays continue as flights resume in US after communications outage | World News - The Indian Express
items.excerpt: Updated: Nov 14, 2026 10:03 AM IST ... The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) allowed domestic flights to resume after a nationwide ground stop lasting more than four hours due to a telecommunications outage that disrupted air traffic control systems, CNN reported. However, flight delays continue as the backlog of departures of grounded flights are cleared. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed ageing technology and overloaded routers, warning that further disruptions could occur unless Congress funds system upgrades, according to the report. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the outage was not caused by a security threat or linked to the recent Microsoft disruption. An estimated 1.5 million passengers were stranded, the report stated. The outage resulted in more than 10,000 flight delays and 5,000 cancellations. Mullin said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Initially, airlines warned that disruptions could continue for days as aircraft, crews and passengers are repositioned. There is, however, no official word on how long the flight delays would continue. It was the longest nationwide flight halt in the US since the September 11, 2001 attacks. ## Trump Cabinet secretary faces pressure over Nvidia crisis US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is now being blamed for part of the Nvidia crisis that allegedly threatened US national security. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Lutnick for failing to ensure appropriate checks on the export of advanced AI chips to Megaspeed, which allegedly had access to Chinese funding. Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, president and board member, on November 12 following reports of two affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by US intelligence of working for Chinese intelligence. The relationship raised national security concerns over potential access to sensitive Nvidia information and Megaspeed’s reported $4.8 billion purchases of Nvidia-powered AI equipment. A third affair came to the fore barely hours after his resignation. Singapore clarified that Alice Huang was investigated for suspected false declarations, not espionage, while China rejected the allegations. Huang’s other reported relationships involved Nvidia vice-president Kimberly Powell and another unidentified employee. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO, while the company completes its investigation. ## SpaceX faces Starship setback as booster explodes; senators seek Musk records on Ukraine Starlink curbs SpaceX’s 15th Starship test flight successfully reached orbit and deployed 26 Starlink satellites on Friday, but its Super Heavy booster exploded over the Gulf of Mexico after failing to complete its planned return. The spacecraft’s upper stage is scheduled to attempt a return landing in Texas on Saturday as part of Elon Musk’s effort to develop a fully reusable rocket. Separately, Democratic US Senators Jeanne Shaheen and Chris Coons have asked Musk to preserve SpaceX records concerning restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starlink and military-grade Starshield services, setting a November 30 deadline for confirmation. The lawmakers cited national security concerns after Ukrainian forces reported communications disruptions affecting frontline operations and drone defence, with President Volodymyr Zelenskiy reporting fresh outages. Trump to hold historic trilateral meeting with Xi, Putin on nuclear weapons US President Donald Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin jointly next week on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, the White House said, marking the first-ever trilateral meeting between leaders of the three countries. The talks are expected to focus on nuclear non-proliferation and reducing nuclear weapons, as well as Iran. However, US officials have cautioned that no agreement is expected, describing the meeting as an initial step towards future discussions. Beijing and Moscow have yet to officially confirm their participation.

items.title: Fed’s Jefferson says he is taking his policy cues from inflation By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Nov 13, 2026, 07:03 PM Updated Nov 13, 2026, 07:12 PM ... Nov 13 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said on Friday that, with the economy growing and the labor market stabilized, he is taking his policy cues from inflation, a remark that suggests he may support further interest-rate hikes to bring it under control. Jefferson joined the 10-2 majority of Fed policymakers who voted at their October meeting to wait for more data to accumulate before considering a rate hike. "Data received since that meeting have been consistent with economic activity and labor market conditions remaining broadly solid, while inflation readings show persistent price pressures," Jefferson said in remarks prepared for delivery at the University of California, San Diego. "Accordingly, I see the trajectory of inflation as providing the more important signal for determining the appropriate stance of monetary policy." Other Fed policymakers in recent weeks have been explicit that elevated and persistent inflation means they would likely support rate hikes that are bigger or come in quicker succession than the single quarter-point increase the Fed delivered in September. Jefferson gave no such guidance. "Going forward, I believe that further policy adjustments should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks," he said.

items.title: Bessent, Fed’s Goolsbee divided on role of energy shock in inflation By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Nov 13, 2026, 09:02 AM Updated Nov 13, 2026, 10:42 AM © Reuters. WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday that the Federal Reserve should not hike rates because of inflation driven by an "energy supply shock" tied to the Iran war, comments made to CNBC and promptly contradicted on the network by Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who said price pressures were building far beyond what could be explained by high oil prices. "I think the Fed should understand that this is an energy supply shock," while the underlying US economy is very strong, Bessent said in an interview on CNBC. "So I think that to hike too much into an energy supply shock when it’s coming down, these are very noisy numbers...You know, the Fed’s supposed to look into the future, not look in the rearview mirror." Shortly afterwards, the network hosted Goolsbee, a regular guest on CNBC’s morning Squawk Box show, who said that inflation was not just due to energy, but had spread to the service sector and areas like medical care that are not usually responsive to the price of oil, and was also elevated through strong demand tied to the AI data center buildout. "I respect the secretary and I am trying to figure out the same thing he is trying to figure out, which is how persistent is this inflation? The tariff inflation and oil price shock were supposed to have gone away by now and it hasn’t," Goolsbee said. "One puzzle is why have those supply shocks been as persistent as they have been. A second thing is if demand is overheating and that is contributing to inflation, that is more worrisome... Services inflation, which is probably not coming from tariffs or oil, is one of the more troubling aspects of the inflation reports we have been getting." While not committing to a rate hike, he said the Fed "has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility." ... Fed policymakers were open to the possibility they could "look through" supply-driven inflation at the start of the US war with Iran. But as inflation remained lodged above the Fed’s target, concern about it grew, as did support for rate hikes. Research meanwhile opened a different window on the relationship between oil prices and US inflation. Because the US is an energy exporter, higher global oil prices can filter through to the economy in the form of higher corporate profits and wages, providing a source of inflation beyond supply issues that can’t be easily ignored by the central bank. Recent stronger-than-expected jobs and inflation reports have further bolstered the case for more Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, and even prompted some officials to discuss the need for a larger-than-typical half-percentage-point increase at the central bank’s coming December 8-9 meeting. "We have had signs of trouble now for several months in a row if you look at how broad-based the inflation is," Goolsbee said. "In categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you are still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way ... That is not going away no matter what happens to the price of oil." "Are we on a path back to 2%? My feeling right now is we are not and we’ve got to deal with that," Goolsbee said. "Conventional wisdom says do everything you can to prevent demand overheating," Goolsbee said, with coming data on inflation the key to whether the Fed needs a faster pace of rate increases.

items.title: The Fed chief said AI would tame inflation. His colleagues disagree. – DNYUZ
items.excerpt: November 14, 2026 in News When President Donald Trump chose him to lead the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh argued that the artificial intelligence boom would help tame inflation. More than a dozen of his colleagues, including two other Trump appointees, now say it’s doing the opposite, playing a role in fueling inflation, which could soon mean even higher interest rates on credit cards, car loans and mortgages. Warsh will get a chance to revisit that argument on Monday, when he opens a conference in San Francisco meant to inform the work of a task force he created to study AI’s effects on jobs and productivity. He heads into it looking increasingly out of step with many other Fed officials. This week, Fed governor Michelle Bowman, a Trump appointee who like Warsh once predicted AI would help push inflation down, conceded that is not yet happening. She said the AI buildout accounts for roughly a quarter of the excess inflation the Fed is fighting, about as much as the pressure from tariffs or energy prices. Fed governor Christopher Waller, who said a big interest rate hike should be on the table in December, on Tuesday pointed to research by Fed economists on AI and high energy prices. Their findings, the Trump appointee said, “do not encourage me to think that these factors will be fading anytime soon.” Hotter-than-expected inflation numbers out this week underscored the concerns raised by Bowman and Waller. Electricity prices jumped in October, and smartphones also logged their largest monthly increase since the government began tracking them separately in 2019. The data center buildout has been driving up electricity prices over the past year, as well as demand for chips that are also critical for consumer electronics. Warsh has acknowledged that the artificial intelligence boom is increasing the price of computer chips, but he has questioned whether it is driving inflation more broadly. “Economic growth is higher, but that doesn’t tell me that economic growth is somehow causing inflation and making our job harder,” he said at his news conference last month after the Fed held rates steady a week before the midterm elections. Warsh said politics played no role in the decision. The debate over AI’s role in inflation comes down to timing. Right now companies racing to build AI are competing for the same chips, electricity and electricians, which pushes prices up. But AI could eventually make businesses more efficient, allowing them to produce more for less and helping hold prices down. If that payoff comes in the near term, as Warsh suggested before he took over the Federal Reserve, the central bank can afford to be patient. If the productivity gains are years away, as many at the Fed now fear, Fed officials may need to keep raising interest rates to cool things off. So far, Warsh’s views haven’t kept the Fed from acting. The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to raise rates in September for the first time in more than three years. Several officials have said they expect another increase at the Fed’s December meeting.

items.title: US October Inflation Beats Forecasts, Complicating Fed’s Rate Path
items.excerpt: The United States economy received an uncomfortable inflation reading this week. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.4% in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, above economists’ forecast of 0.3%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, climbed 0.3% for the third consecutive month, also exceeding expectations of a 0.2% increase. Several categories contributed to the monthly rise: - Shelter costs increased 0.3%, accounting for more than 30% of the monthly CPI increase. - Food prices jumped 0.5%, driven by higher costs for snacks, beef, and dairy. - Transportation services surged 0.8%, while airline fares rose 0.4%. The report adds pressure on the Federal Reserve ahead of its December policy meeting, with markets increasingly pricing in another interest rate hike before year-end. In a historic twist, the BLS did not publish an annual inflation rate. A government shutdown in October 2025 prevented data collection. On a three-month annualized basis, total CPI is running at 5.7%, its fastest pace since May 2026.

items.excerpt: November 13, 2026, 10:20 PM EST ... ## Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months The federal government today announced a six-month delay in enforcing a Medicaid work requirement — a central provision in Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” that experts said would lead millions of Americans to lose health coverage. The requirement still technically starts on Jan. 1, but under new guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, states that choose not to enforce it won’t be held accountable until at least July 1. The move is a striking turn for an administration that has spent months defending the policy against criticism from state officials and healthcare advocates who warned that the rollout was moving too quickly and that people who should be eligible for Medicaid would lose coverage because of the additional red tape and paperwork. CMS called the six-month window a “hold harmless” period, and the delay is optional. States that choose to take advantage of this period will still start checking on Jan. 1 whether Medicaid enrollees are working, volunteering or in school or whether they qualify for an exemption. But until July, no one in those states will lose coverage for failing to meet the requirements. ... ## Transportation Sec. Get ready for all the Slime, Music and Mayhem with our handy guide to KCA 2026! | | | --- | | Courtesy of Nickelodeon | Multiplatinum GRAMMY ® Award-nominated global superstar Alex Warren is set to take the stage as host of CBS PRESENTS NICKELODEON KIDS’ CHOICE AWARDS (“KCAs”). Celebrating fans’ favorites from across the worlds of film, television, music, gaming, sports and more, the “KCAs” will broadcast live from Television City in Los Angeles on Saturday, Nov. 14 (8:00-9:30 PM, ET/5:00-6:30 PM, PT), airing for the first time on CBS Television Network and Nickelodeon, and streaming live on Paramount+ for Premium subscribers and on-demand the next day for both Premium and Essential subscribers in the U.S. The show will also be available globally on Nickelodeon and Paramount+ following its linear premiere on Nickelodeon in the U.S. Breakout music sensation Jamie Miller will kick off the show with the U.S. television debut performance of his #1 viral hit song “Babydoll.” Featuring a cast of dancers and a cameo by JYT, the high-energy opening number will celebrate some of pop culture’s most memorable dance crazes across the decades before culminating in Miller’s performance, which includes special appearances by Antonio Cipriano and Victoria Justice, setting the tone for an unforgettable night of music, slime and surprises. Paying tribute to iconic dance moments, spanning from the 1980s to today, the first “KCAs” act will feature a medley of memorable hits, including “Rhythm Nation” (Janet Jackson, 1980s), “Everybody” (Backstreet Boys, 1990s), “Just Dance” (Lady Gaga, 2000s), “Gangnam Style” (PSY, 2010s) and “Which One” (JYT, 2026). Multiplatinum singer-songwriter Ashe and GRAMMY ® -nominated electronic music duo SOFI TUKKER will bring two of the year’s most buzzworthy tracks to the celebration. Ashe will perform her breakout hit “Stop the Wedding!” while SOFI TUKKER will bring their fan-favorite dance anthem “TSUNAMI,” the duo’s collaboration with Ryan Tedder. KING OF COMEDY AWARD: Chris Pratt will receive the iconic King of Comedy Award. He will receive the coveted Silver Blimp in celebration of his career, before facing Nickelodeon’s iconic slime. PARTICIPANTS: Look out for a raft of special appearances from your favorite stars, including from: Alysa Liu, Alyssa Miles, Daniella Monet, Dixie D’Amelio, Ginnifer Goodwin, Howie Mandel, Ice Spice, Jack Griffo, Jackson Olson, Jerry Trainor, Jude Hill, Keke Palmer, Kira Kosarin, Matthew Gray Gubler, Meg Donnelly, Milo Manheim, Quinta Brunson, Salish Matter, SeanDoesMagic, Stella Lefty, Teyana Taylor, Taylen Biggs, Tony Hawk and Tyler James Williams NOMINATIONS: Taylor Swift leads all individual nominees with six nods. Other top nominees include Ariana Grande (5) and Sabrina Carpenter (5). Blockbuster franchises dominate this year’s ballot, with fan-favorite worlds including “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie,” “Toy Story 5,” “Wednesday,” “Wicked: For Good,” THE SPONGEBOB MOVIE: SEARCH FOR SQUAREPANTS, “KPop Demon Hunters” and “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” represented across multiple categories. Music’s biggest stars remain a major force with BTS, Olivia Rodrigo, Bruno Mars, Justin Bieber, Cardi B and Karol G earning nominations across artist, song, album and collaboration categories. New categories this year are Watch Party: Kids’ Choice, Favorite On-Screen Duo/Trio and Favorite Clutch Player of the Year.
